meta: Robert Campin's John the Baptist, about 1410, probably the right wing of a triptych and cut down along the lower edge.
about: John the Baptist wears a hair shirt under a white cloth, which the Cleveland Museum of Art ties to newly baptized Christians. He holds a flag with a red cross, a sign of resurrection, and behind him hangs a lavish gold-patterned silk. The panel has been cut down at the bottom and once showed the saint at full length. It was probably the right wing of a triptych, with John looking toward a central image of the Virgin and Child. Campin settled in Tournai around 1405 as a master of the painters' guild and bought citizenship there in 1410.
credit_line: Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust

meta: Abraham Janssens's Jupiter Rebuked by Venus, about 1612, an Antwerp mythology painting that echoes a Raphael ceiling in Rome.
about: Venus reprimands a visibly annoyed Jupiter on Mount Olympus while Cupid and a crowd of onlookers gather around. The Art Institute of Chicago says the composition echoes one by Raphael on the ceiling of the Villa Farnesina in Rome. Janssens, Rubens's main competitor in Antwerp in the 1610s, had spent five years in Rome and liked to quote ancient sculpture and Italian Renaissance painting. He made the figures more powerful by stressing their muscles and working on a larger scale. The painting was offered for sale in London in 1902 as a work by Luca Giordano and was bought in.
credit_line: Purchased with funds provided by The Old Masters Society; the Alexander A. McKay Endowment

meta: Kano Motonobu's Flowers and Birds in a Spring Landscape, a 1500s sliding-door painting now mounted as a hanging scroll.
about: White plum blossoms cover a gnarled tree trunk where small birds perch, with bamboo leaves and a rocky outcrop at the lower right. It is one of four paintings that first decorated sliding doors dividing the rooms of Japanese buildings. The Cleveland Museum of Art credits Kano Motonobu with combining the subtlety of Chinese black ink painting, seen in the rocks and hills, with the color and realism of Japanese painting, seen in the birds and flowers. Landscapes like this were prized by the elite of Kyoto for their contemplative quality.

meta: Ren Bonian's hanging scroll of Zhong Kui, the Demon Queller, here an elegant if eccentric scholar.
about: A bearded figure in a flowing red robe sits beside a bamboo table with vases of flowering branches and scrolls. He is Zhong Kui, the legendary Demon Queller. The accompanying text calls the artist Ren Yi, a leader of the late Qing Shanghai school and a disciple of Ren Xiong. Here he adopted the figure style of Chen Hongshou. In the late Qing, Zhong Kui was often drawn glowering over cowering ghosts and demons, as a symbol of opposition to Manchu misrule. Ren Yi's Zhong Kui is an elegant if somewhat eccentric scholar with his sword sheathed and a blossom stuck in his hair.

meta: Simone Martini's Saint Simon, about 1315 to 1320, one of ten panels of a series later split up between Cologne and Washington.
about: Under an arched frame, a bearded saint in a green mantle holds a closed book with metal clasps against a gold ground. His name is written beside him as SANCTUS SYMON. The panel belongs to a series of ten. Johann Anton Ramboux of Cologne acquired it between 1832 and 1842, apparently in Siena, along with other panels. His estate sale offered all ten as the work of Lippo Memmi. The Wallraf-Richartz-Museum in Cologne bought the series and later sold it, and Philip Lehman of New York ended up with four panels. The Kress Foundation gave them to the National Gallery in 1952.
dimensions:
painted surface: 26.2 x 19.7 cm (10 5/16 x 7 3/4 in.)
overall: 30.7 x 23.5 cm (12 1/16 x 9 1/4 in.)
framed: 44.4 x 60 cm (17 1/2 x 23 5/8 in.)

meta: Benvenuto di Giovanni's Adoration of the Magi, about 1470 to 1475, once sold as a work by Gentile da Fabriano.
about: The Virgin sits holding the Christ Child while kneeling kings in patterned gold and red garments offer gifts, with a stable and an ox and donkey at the left. When the collection of Giuseppe Toscanelli of Pontedera and Pisa was sold in 1883, the panel was catalogued as the work of Gentile da Fabriano. It went on to Sir William Neville Abdy and then to his daughter, Lady Abdy, whose sale in London in 1911 again gave it to Gentile. Dealers including Charles Sedelmeyer and Duveen Brothers handled it before the Mellon trust bought it in 1936.

meta: Matteo di Giovanni's Madonna and Child with Saint Jerome, Saint Catherine of Alexandria and Angels, about 1465 to 1470.
about: In a red brocade gown and deep blue mantle, the Virgin Mary holds the Christ Child between an elderly bearded saint with an open book and a woman holding a book, with an angel peering from behind. Words in her halo read AVE GRATIA PLENA DOMINUS TECUM, the angel's greeting from the Gospel of Luke. The panel may once have belonged to the earls of Ashburnham, who lived at Ashburnham Place in Sussex. Robert Langton Douglas sold it to Duveen Brothers in 1919, and the American collector Clarence H. Mackay bought it in 1922. The Kress Foundation acquired it in 1938.

meta: Joseph Blackburn's Portrait of a Gentleman, about 1760, signed I: Blackburn Pinx and acquired by the National Gallery of Art in 2014.
about: Before a column and a landscape under a cloudy sky stands a man in a brown coat with silver braided trim and a pale blue waistcoat embroidered with silver flowers. Blackburn signed the portrait at center left with I: Blackburn Pinx. The John Nicholson Gallery in New York showed it first in 1958. Charles Childs of Boston and a dealer in Hartsville, South Carolina, handled it next. The Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington bought it, and the National Gallery of Art acquired it from the Corcoran in 2014.

meta: John William Casilear's 1857 View on Lake George, a hazy lake scene that stayed in the Sturges family for three generations.
about: A broad lake lies in hazy sunlight between wooded slopes and rocky cliffs, with a distant peak at the center. A seated figure rests on the rocks beside a path, and a small boat drifts on the water. Casilear monogrammed the canvas JWC and dated it 57. The painting possibly belonged to the New York collector Jonathan Sturges and then passed to his son Frederick, and on to Frederick Sturges Jr. of Fairfield, Connecticut. It came to the National Gallery of Art as a gift in 1978.

meta: Anthony Oberman's Two Riders in a Landscape, 1817, on loan to the Rijksmuseum from the City of Amsterdam.
about: Waiting on a white dappled horse, a woman in a dark blue cloak watches while a man standing beside his own horse adjusts its bridle. Behind them, rolling fields and trees run toward a distant farmhouse. Oberman signed and dated the painting at lower left. It reached the museum as a loan from the City of Amsterdam, part of the A. van der Hoop Bequest.

meta: Wybrand de Geest's Self-Portrait, 1629, a bust with a white lace ruff and gold chain, made as a pendant to another portrait.
about: Wybrand de Geest painted himself in bust length, turned to the right, with reddish hair and a beard, a black doublet and a thin gold chain over a large white lace ruff. The Rijksmuseum treats it as a pendant to another portrait in its collection. The date at the upper left is written in pale green Roman numerals. Both paintings came to the museum in 1898 from Dr. R. Hoornsma Cannegieter of Donkerbroek, and since 1948 the pair has been on loan to the Fries Museum in Leeuwarden.

meta: George Pieter Westenberg's 1817 winter view of the Whetstone Market in Amsterdam and the building Het Zeerecht.
about: Snow covers the streets and buildings of the Whetstone Market in Amsterdam, where a man walks a dog on the left. Ships lie at the quay. The Rijksmuseum names the large building as Het Zeerecht on the Buitenkant. Gabled brick houses stand on the left of the view and a small building with a snowy roof on the right, and bare trees frame the center. Westenberg signed and dated the painting at lower right.

meta: Willem Bartel van der Kooi's 1791 self-portrait pointing at a portrait of his late colleague Dirk Jacobsz Ploegsma.
about: The painter stands half-length in an olive coat and points toward a portrait of his dead colleague Dirk Jacobsz Ploegsma, who holds a palette and brushes. Above the portrait a mourning allegorical figure, perhaps Painting, appears together with Fame, according to the Rijksmuseum. Ploegsma lived only from 1769 to 1791. A painted curtain and classical figures frame the scene against a dark background.

meta: Jean-Joseph-Xavier Bidauld's The Bridge at La Cava, Kingdom of Naples, 1778, sold at auction in 2001 and later owned by Eugene V. Thaw.
about: An arched stone bridge crosses a river in the foreground, with a multi-story building and bell tower on the left and rolling hills under a pale evening sky. The painting may have been in Bidauld's own estate sale in Paris in 1847, listed either as a view of the bridge and hospital or as a view of the bridge and part of the town. A private collector later owned it, and his son sold it at Sotheby's in New York in 2001 as A View of the Acqueduct near the Villa de la Cava. Eugene V. Thaw of New York bought it afterward.

meta: Giovanni Battista Naldini's 1570 red chalk study of heads of a man, a woman and a child, with a profile copied from an antique statue.
about: Heads fill this red chalk sheet. At the upper left a man's head turns to the right, and at the upper right is a woman's profile that Naldini copied from an antique statue. A child sits upright in the center as if in bed, and a second child's head, seen from three-quarter front, looks upward beside it.

meta: Joseph Badger's 1755 portrait of Eleanor Wyer, wife of Isaac Foster, with an inscription on the back of the original canvas.
about: Seated against a dark background, a woman in a gray gown with white lace cuffs and a white lace cap tied with a blue ribbon looks straight at the viewer. On the back of the original canvas an inscription names her Eleanor, only daughter of William Wyer and his wife Eleanor. By 1873 the portrait belonged to Mrs. David Buffum of Walpole, New Hampshire. Her son Dr. Thomas Bellows Buffum owned it later, and then Annie Buffum Williams of Northampton, Massachusetts. Edgar William and Bernice Chrysler Garbisch bought it in Boston and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1957.
credit_line: Gift of Edgar William and Bernice Chrysler Garbisch

meta: Aertgen Claesz van Leyden's The Calling of Saint Anthony, 1530, a church sermon with Anthony standing among the listeners.
about: In a church, a priest in a surplice preaches from the pulpit to a gathered crowd of seated and standing men and women. On the wall behind him hangs a painting of Moses with the Ten Commandments, and flowers are strewn on the floor in front. At the far right Saint Anthony listens beside five other men, whom the Rijksmuseum guesses may be donors. In the background he hands out bread to the poor, beggars and the lame. Anthony appears twice. The artist marked the panel with an L monogram at lower right.

meta: Ambrosius Bosschaert's 1606 Flowers in a Glass, a bouquet in a faceted vase with a snail, a butterfly and a dragonfly.
about: Tulips and irises stand in a faceted glass vase on a pale ledge against a dark ground. Roses and lilies rise among them. Small creatures sit in the bouquet. Look for the snail, the caterpillar, the butterfly and the dragonfly. The museum text calls Bosschaert one of the first artists to specialize in flower painting. It says he may have been inspired by the botanical gardens and scientific collections of his hometown, Middelburg. Flowers that seem common now were costly rarities in the 1600s.
